{{Short description|Type of data visualization}}
[[File:Andrews curve for Iris data set.png|thumb|360px|An Andrews curve for the Iris data set]]

In [[data visualization]], an '''Andrews plot''' or '''Andrews curve''' is a way to visualize structure in high-dimensional data. It is basically a rolled-down, non-integer version of the Kent–Kiviat [[radar chart|radar m chart]], or a smoothed version of a [[parallel coordinates|parallel coordinate plot]]. It is named after the statistician David F. Andrews.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Andrews |first=D. F. |date=1972 |title=Plots of High-Dimensional Data |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2528964 |journal=Biometrics |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=125–136 |doi=10.2307/2528964|jstor=2528964 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Embrechts |first1=Paul |last2=Herzberg |first2=Agnes M. |date=1991 |title=Variations of Andrews' Plots |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1403442 |journal=International Statistical Review / Revue Internationale de Statistique |volume=59 |issue=2 |pages=175–194 |doi=10.2307/1403442 |jstor=1403442 |issn=0306-7734|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Visualization of High-Dimensional Data via Orthogonal Curves |first1=César |last1=García-Osorio |first2=Colin |last2=Fyfe |journal=Journal of Universal Computer Science |volume=11 |issue=11 |year=2005 |pages=1806–1819 |url=http://www.jucs.org/jucs_11_11/visualization_of_high_dimensional/jucs_11_11_1806_1819_garc_a_osorio.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |work=Rip’s Applied Mathematics Blog |title=Andrews Curves |date=3 October 2011 |url=http://rip94550.wordpress.com/2011/10/03/andrews-curves/}}</ref>

A value <math> x </math> is a [[Real coordinate space|high-dimensional datapoint]] if it is an element of <math>\mathbb R ^d </math>. We can represent high-dimensional data with a number for each of their dimensions,  <math>x = \left \{ x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_d \right \}</math>.  To visualize them, the Andrews plot  defines a finite [[Fourier series]]:

: <math>f_x(t) = \frac{x_1}{\sqrt 2} + x_2 \sin(t) + x_3 \cos(t) + x_4 \sin(2t) + x_5 \cos(2t) + \cdots</math>

This function is then plotted for <math>-\pi < t < \pi</math>. Thus each data point may be viewed as a line between <math>-\pi</math> and <math>\pi</math>. This formula can be thought of as the projection of the data point onto the vector:

: <math>\left ( \frac 1 {\sqrt 2}, \sin(t), \cos(t), \sin(2t), \cos(2t), \ldots \right ) </math>

If there is structure in the data, it may be visible in the Andrews curves of the data.

These curves have been utilized in fields as different as [[biology]], [[neurology]], [[sociology]] and [[semiconductor]] manufacturing. Some of their uses include the [[quality control]] of products, the detection of period and [[outlier]]s in [[time series]], the visualization of learning in [[artificial neural network]]s, and correspondence analysis.

Theoretically, it is possible to project them onto an [[n-sphere|''n''-sphere]]. The projection onto the circle results in the aforementioned [[radar chart]].
